product: SmartCiti.X : Trade Craft Academy (powered by AGI Corp)
guarantee: cosmetic only: every option is free and unlocked, and no avatar choice affects scoring, access, progression or anything the rubrics measure
provenance: AUTHORED - every part, colour, name and note in this locker is typed from general public knowledge of the trades and is not cross-checked against any standard this build can read. A note says what a piece of kit is FOR; it is not the standard, not a specification, and not a substitute for the qualified person on site. Nothing here is RECORDED, and nothing here is graded.
gestures: the emotes are gestures an avatar plays on a pedestal. The hoist, lower and stop shapes borrow the yard’s own hand vocabulary because it is the vocabulary members learn, but playing one here is not a signalperson qualification and confers nothing: on a real lift only the qualified signalperson signals, and anyone may call a stop.
marks: crew marks are the Academy’s own insignia - the roster’s three-letter hall codes on a shield in the district hue, the same codes the campus map prints. They are not, and do not imitate, any real union’s logo or emblem; no local is named and none is drawn. The animal mascots are original Academy characters drawn from scratch in this page’s own primitive style; they are not, and do not imitate, any third-party character, collection or brand - no Bored Ape or other NFT artwork is reproduced or derived from.

ape_reference.provenance: measured from a user-supplied GLB; measurements only - the mesh is not shipped, no geometry or texture is copied, and no third-party artwork is derived from

tradeapes.honesty: an original Academy collection, generated from the roster itself - one ape per hall, free and cosmetic only. Not tokens: nothing is an NFT, nothing is for sale, and no blockchain is involved. Original art: no third-party ape artwork, collection or brand is imitated.

options.name: Bare head
options.note: No head protection: the classroom, the office and the locker, and nowhere a hard-hat sign is posted.

options.name: Cap-style hard hat
options.note: The everyday shell against the falling object and the low steel overhead.

options.name: Full-brim hard hat
options.note: A brim all the way round carries rain and sun off the neck as well as taking the overhead hit.

options.name: Climbing-style helmet
options.note: A chin strap and a deeper shell, for work at height where a hat that comes off is a hat that is gone.

options.name: Old-pattern shell
options.note: The tall pre-war shell, kept for the parade and the photographs rather than the deck.

options.name: Composite shell
options.note: A light shell for the long shift, where the weight of the hat is the complaint by hour eight.

options.name: Ball cap
options.note: Cloth only: sun off the face where nothing overhead can fall.

options.name: Ball cap, reversed
options.note: Worn backwards so a welding hood, a face shield or a scope can sit square.

options.name: Flat cap
options.note: Cloth and low-brimmed, for the shop and the walk to it.

options.name: Beanie
options.note: Knit warmth for cold work with no overhead hazard.

options.name: Bucket hat
options.note: Brimmed all round against sun and glare on open ground, the survey line included.

options.name: Welding cap
options.note: A cotton crown under the hood, taking spark and spatter off the scalp.

options.name: Visor
options.note: Brim and sweatband with the crown left open, for heat and glare indoors.

options.name: Headband
options.note: Keeps sweat out of the eyes and off the inside of a safety lens.

options.name: Bandana
options.note: Cloth over the scalp, worn under the hood or under the shell.

options.name: Winter liner
options.note: An insulated liner for cold work; on site it belongs under a shell, not instead of one.

options.name: Vented hard hat
options.note: Vents for heat, and conductive by design: a vented shell carries no electrical rating.

options.name: Hard hat over liner
options.note: The cold-weather assembly: the insulated liner underneath, the shell still doing the protecting.

options.name: Hard hat with sun shade
options.note: A brim-and-neck shade clipped to the shell, for open ground in heat-illness weather.

options.name: Bump cap
options.note: A thin shell for pipe racks and low clearances; it is not impact-rated and never stands in for a hard hat.

options.name: Coveralls
options.note: One piece over the clothes, keeping dust and spatter off what goes home in the truck.

options.name: Hi-vis tee
options.note: High-visibility in short sleeve; a short-sleeved garment cannot carry the highest visibility class on its own.

options.name: Thermal base layer
options.note: The layer under everything else when the work is cold and standing still.

options.name: Rain shell
options.note: A waterproof layer over the working clothes for a wet shift.

options.name: Flame-resistant shirt
options.note: Daily wear where a flash fire or an arc is possible, so the shirt does not melt into the burn.

options.name: Hi-vis long sleeve
options.note: Sleeved high-visibility, the piece a top-class ensemble needs and a vest alone cannot supply.

options.name: Sun hoodie
options.note: A light hooded sun shirt: cover beats sunscreen across a ten-hour outdoor shift.

options.name: Smock
options.note: A lint-controlled layer for cleanroom and finishing work, where the hazard is what the member sheds.

options.name: No vest
options.note: Shop and indoor work, where nothing moving has to see you first.

options.name: Hi-vis, lowest class
options.note: The least background material and tape, for off-road work away from moving traffic.

options.name: Hi-vis, roadway class
options.note: The roadway vest: more background and tape, for traffic and for plant yards where equipment moves.

options.name: Hi-vis, highest class
options.note: The largest vest in the rack, worn with sleeves or hi-vis trousers to make the highest-class ensemble for night work.

options.name: Surveyor vest
options.note: Vertical tape and pockets deep enough for a field book and a prism.

options.name: Fall-arrest harness
options.note: Full-body harness with the dorsal D-ring between the shoulder blades, which is the fall-arrest ring.

options.name: Positioning harness
options.note: Hip D-rings for leaning back on rebar or a pole; work positioning is not fall arrest and needs its own line.

options.name: Retrieval harness
options.note: Shoulder D-rings for a vertical lift, the harness an attendant hauls an entrant out of a hole with.

options.name: Ladder-climb harness
options.note: A sternal D-ring at the chest for a ladder rail or cable climb system.

options.name: Tool vest
options.note: Pockets instead of a belt, for ladder and lift work where a loaded belt drags on the hips.

options.name: Mesh vest
options.note: Open mesh for heat: the same visibility with air moving through it.

options.name: Insulated vest
options.note: A lined vest for cold work that keeps the arms free to move.

options.name: Flame-resistant vest
options.note: For work near an ignition source, where an ordinary vest is itself the burn.

options.name: Crew shell
options.note: A light shell in the hall’s colours: a garment for the hall and the ride in, with nothing protective in it.

options.name: Rain vest
options.note: A coated shell over the torso for wet work with the arms left free.

options.name: Lead apron
options.note: For radiographic weld inspection, the shot everyone else clears the area for.

options.name: Life vest
options.note: Buoyancy for work over water: the dock edge, the barge and the bridge pier.

options.name: Back support
options.note: A belt and brace: a reminder of lifting technique, and not a permit to lift more.

options.name: Insulated outer vest
options.note: An outer layer for cold open ground with the sleeves of the work shirt underneath.

options.name: Cooling vest
options.note: A phase-change or evaporative vest for heat-illness weather worked in full protective equipment.

options.name: Insulated trousers
options.note: Lined trousers for cold standing work, where movement will not keep a body warm.

options.name: Rain trousers
options.note: Waterproof over-trousers for standing water and wet ground.

options.name: Hi-vis trousers
options.note: High-visibility on the legs, which is where a member is seen from in a machine mirror.

options.name: Painter's whites
options.note: The trade uniform of the painters, and a surface that shows the day’s work on it.

options.name: Flame-resistant trousers
options.note: For arc and flash-fire work, so the trousers do not keep burning after the source is gone.

options.name: Hi-vis trousers, ensemble class
options.note: Not a class on their own: worn with a roadway vest they make the highest-class ensemble.

options.name: Knee-pad trousers
options.note: Built-in knee pockets for the trades that work the whole day off their knees.

options.name: Saw chaps
options.note: Cut-resistant chaps for chainsaw work: the fibres pull out and jam the chain.

options.name: Hip waders
options.note: For the wet trench, the treatment plant and shallow water work.

options.name: Steel toe, brown
options.note: The ordinary work boot: a steel toe against impact and compression.

options.name: Steel toe, black
options.note: The same toe in black, for the shops and plants whose dress code asks for it.

options.name: Steel toe, tan
options.note: The first pair most apprentices buy, and the one they learn to re-lace.

options.name: Composite toe
options.note: A non-metallic toe: nothing to set off a detector, and nothing to carry the cold in.

options.name: Logger boot
options.note: A high shaft and an aggressive sole for broken ground and saw work.

options.name: Wellington
options.note: Pull-on and slip-resistant, for wet concrete and washdown floors.

options.name: Work hiker
options.note: A light boot for survey lines and days measured in miles walked.

options.name: Chemical rubber boot
options.note: Chemical-resistant rubber for the wash bay and the spill.

options.name: Water rubber boot
options.note: Rubber for water work: wet trench, treatment plant and dock.

options.name: White trainers
options.note: Street shoes: no toe cap and no rating, so the hall and the classroom only.

options.name: Black trainers
options.note: The pair that passes a shop-floor dress code and no toe-protection rule anywhere.

options.name: Red trainers
options.note: Trainers in a crew colour, for the hall and the bus, with nothing protective in them.

options.name: Blue trainers
options.note: The pair kept in the locker for the walk home once the boots come off.

options.name: High tops
options.note: Laced over the ankle for support, still with nothing on the toe.

options.name: Slip-on
options.note: Quick off at the door of a clean space, and quick on again.

options.name: Lineman boot
options.note: A tall lace-up with a shank cut to take a climber and a pole gaff.

options.name: Metatarsal guard
options.note: An external guard over the laces, for the drop and the pour that lands on the instep.

options.name: Electrical-hazard boot
options.note: A secondary barrier against step potential; it is not an insulator and does not make a circuit safe to touch.

options.name: Puncture-resistant sole
options.note: A plate under the foot for demolition floors and nail-strewn decking.

options.name: Insulated pac boot
options.note: For standing on frozen ground through a whole winter shift.

options.name: No belt
options.note: The walk-through, the classroom, and the lift basket where a loaded belt snags on the rail.

options.name: Basic belt
options.note: Tape, knife and one pouch: what everybody carries in week one.

options.name: Framing belt
options.note: Hammer, speed square and nail bags for wood framing.

options.name: Electrician belt
options.note: Side cutters, strippers and a voltage tester on the hip.

options.name: Plumber belt
options.note: Wrenches, a tubing cutter and a striker for the torch.

options.name: Mason belt
options.note: Trowels, line blocks and a brick hammer, all of it wiped before the mud sets.

options.name: Welder belt
options.note: Chipping hammer, wire brush, soapstone and tip cleaners.

options.name: Surveyor belt
options.note: Plumb bob, field book, marking keel and the lath the stakes are cut from.

options.name: Drywall belt
options.note: Taping knives in three widths, a rasp and a banjo full of tape.

options.name: HVAC belt
options.note: Manifold gauges, a fin comb, nut drivers and a thermometer that reads fast.

options.name: Glazier belt
options.note: Suction cups, glazing knives and setting blocks.

options.name: Roofer belt
options.note: Hatchet, seam roller and a nail stripper, carried up a ladder one-handed.

options.name: Concrete belt
options.note: Float, edger and jointer within reach of the pour.

options.name: Rigger belt
options.note: Shackles, a spud wrench and the tags that go on every sling.

options.name: Finisher belt
options.note: Sanding pads, a corner tool and a spare gun tip.

options.name: Lineman belt
options.note: A body belt with climbers, a hand line and a loop for the hot stick.

options.name: Sheet metal belt
options.note: Snips in three cuts, a hand seamer and a scratch awl.

options.name: Painter belt
options.note: A five-in-one, a pot hook, brushes, and more rags than anyone else carries.

options.name: Millwright belt
options.note: Dial indicator, feeler gauges and shim stock for alignment.

options.name: Low-voltage belt
options.note: Punch-down tool, fish tape and a fibre cleaver for structured cabling.

options.name: No outer layer
options.note: Indoor work and the shoulder seasons, when the shirt is the whole answer.

options.name: Parka
options.note: A lined hooded coat for cold open ground, cut long enough to sit down in.

options.name: Rain slicker
options.note: A coated slicker for a long shift in standing rain.

options.name: Welding jacket
options.note: Leather across the shoulders and arms against spatter and arc.

options.name: Bomber jacket
options.note: A short lined jacket cut to clear a tool belt.

options.name: Duster
options.note: A long coat for wind on open sites, where the cold comes sideways.

options.name: Windbreaker
options.note: An unlined shell for wind without the weight.

options.name: Lined flannel
options.note: The shirt-jacket that comes off by ten in the morning.

options.name: Hi-vis parka
options.note: A hooded coat that keeps the visibility class on through winter.

options.name: Softshell
options.note: A stretch shell for cool dry work with a lot of reaching in it.

options.name: Chore canvas
options.note: Duck canvas that takes the abrasion of the yard.

options.name: Puffer
options.note: Insulation for still, cold air where wind is not the problem.

options.name: Anorak
options.note: A pull-over hooded shell with the pocket on the chest.

options.name: Hall jacket
options.note: The crew jacket: the parade, the hall and the ride in.

options.name: Trench coat
options.note: A long coat for the walk between buildings and the wait at the gate.

options.name: Arc-rated coat
options.note: Worn where an arc flash is possible; the whole layer system has to be arc-rated, not this coat alone.

options.name: Heated liner
options.note: A battery-heated layer for standing work in cold, where the body is not generating its own heat.

options.name: Chemical splash coat
options.note: A coated coat for washdown, spill response and anything that sprays back off the surface.

options.name: Cape sleeves
options.note: Leather over the shoulders and arms for overhead welding, where the spatter comes straight down.

options.name: Insulated coverall
options.note: One insulated piece over everything else for the coldest outdoor shifts.

options.name: Nothing extra
options.note: The outfit as it stands, with no additional protective equipment on it.

options.name: Safety glasses
options.note: Impact-rated lenses, the one piece worn gate to gate on most sites.

options.name: Prescription safety glasses
options.note: Impact-rated lenses ground to a prescription, so correction and protection are the same pair.

options.name: Sunglasses
options.note: Tint for glare on open ground and water; a tint is not an impact rating.

options.name: Ear muffs
options.note: Over the ear, on and off quickly around intermittent noise.

options.name: Ear plugs
options.note: Plugs fit under a welding hood and a tight hard-hat band where muffs will not.

options.name: Filtering facepiece
options.note: The lowest class: a disposable facepiece for nuisance dust, and it still needs a seal.

options.name: Half-mask respirator
options.note: Cartridges chosen for the hazard, on a seal that has to be fit-tested to the face wearing it.

options.name: Full-face respirator
options.note: A full facepiece: eye protection and a higher protection factor for abatement work.

options.name: Powered hood
options.note: Powered air into a loose hood - the class that works over facial hair, where a tight-fitting mask cannot seal.

options.name: Supplied air
options.note: Air from a line or a cylinder for confined space and blasting, where filtering the air is not enough.

options.name: Face shield
options.note: Against splash and flying chips, worn over safety glasses and never instead of them.

options.name: Welding shield
options.note: A filter lens against arc flash, and cover against the burn on face and neck.

options.name: Knee pads
options.note: Padding for the trades that spend the day kneeling on concrete.

options.name: Elbow pads
options.note: Padding for overhead and crawlspace work that rides on the elbows.

options.name: Tool lanyard
options.note: A tether, so a dropped tool does not become a falling object.

options.name: Hand radio
options.note: The crew channel on the chest, where it can be heard over plant noise.

options.name: Headlamp
options.note: Hands-free light for the bore, the crawlspace and the night pour.

options.name: Site badge
options.note: Which crew, which gate, and which orientation was sat through.

options.name: Gloves
options.note: Chosen for the hazard: cut, chemical and rubber insulating gloves are not interchangeable.

characters.name: The High-Steel Walker
characters.blurb: Connects iron forty storeys up and never hurries.

characters.name: The Wharf Operator
characters.blurb: Reads the river, the wind, and the manifest before coffee.

characters.name: Night Shift
characters.blurb: The city sleeps; the reflective crew does not.

characters.name: The Line of Sight
characters.blurb: A surveyor’s patience: measure twice, argue never.

characters.name: Sparks
characters.blurb: Finds the fault before the fault finds anyone.

characters.name: Krewe Royalty
characters.blurb: Second line in front, toolbox in back - laissez les bons temps.

characters.name: Foundry Heat
characters.blurb: Walks the pour line where the air itself glows.

characters.name: The Deep Diver
characters.blurb: Inspects the pilings nobody else will ever see.

characters.name: The '33 Crew
characters.blurb: Dressed like the bridge-raisers in the old photographs.

characters.name: Storm Rider
characters.blurb: First truck in after the wind, last one out.

characters.name: The Golden Journey
characters.blurb: Fifty years on the tools, and the hat to prove it.

characters.name: Clean Sweep
characters.blurb: Hazmat-calm in places with warning signs on the doors.

characters.name: Arc Guard
characters.blurb: Suited for the flash that must never happen.

characters.name: The Tunnel Runner
characters.blurb: Knows the bore by sound alone, headlamp always on.

characters.name: Parade Marshal
characters.blurb: Leads the apprentice class down Canal Street once a year.

characters.name: Day One
characters.blurb: New boots, clean gloves, and every question worth asking.

characters.name: Wrench
characters.blurb: The workshop ape - an original Academy mascot who tightens everything twice.

characters.name: The Attendant
characters.blurb: Stands at the hole the whole shift and never once goes in.

characters.name: The Dry Cut
characters.blurb: Argues for water on the blade before anyone starts cutting.

characters.name: The Heat Index
characters.blurb: Watches the index, calls the shade break, takes it first.

characters.name: The Cold Pour
characters.blurb: Pours at twenty degrees and blankets it before the light goes.

characters.name: The Hot Stick
characters.blurb: Works it live from the bucket, and checks the cover-up twice.

emotes.label: Wave
emotes.note: A hand up across the yard.

emotes.label: Thumbs up
emotes.note: Understood - the answer that carries over plant noise.

emotes.label: Point
emotes.note: Points at the thing being talked about.

emotes.label: Hat tip
emotes.note: Hat off and back on, the oldest greeting on a site.

emotes.label: Flex
emotes.note: The end of a hard lift.

emotes.label: Spin
emotes.note: A turn on the spot, to be seen from every side.

emotes.label: Safety check
emotes.note: A hop, for a walk-around that came back clean.

emotes.label: Hoist
emotes.note: The raise shape: forearm up, finger turning.

emotes.label: Lower
emotes.note: The lower shape: arm out and down, finger turning.

emotes.label: Stop
emotes.note: The stop shape: arm out, palm down, swept across.

emotes.label: Tie off
emotes.note: Clipping the lanyard on before stepping out.
